questions.q: A writer's play about a recurring family pattern keeps failing as a cause-and-effect arc. Which teacher would most directly suggest trying a repetitive or circular form instead?
questions.explain: Vogel teaches several plot forms beyond the Aristotelian arc, including circular, backward and repetitive.

questions.q: Which pairing of plot form and example matches Vogel's teaching as Ruhl reports it?
questions.explain: Pinter's Betrayal runs in reverse; La Ronde is circular; Godot is repetitive.

questions.q: What does Vogel mean by saying form and content can't be separated?
choices: The structure is part of the meaning, not a neutral container
questions.explain: A memory play might be built like memory; a play about recurrence might repeat.

questions.q: How does How I Learned to Drive's structure do its work?
choices: Scenes jump between ages and the earliest, most painful memory is held back until near the end
Each scene is introduced by songs
questions.explain: Time works backwards: the late revelation changes how the audience reads what came before.

questions.q: Vogel draws on Shklovsky's idea of making the familiar strange. What is it called?
questions.explain: Compare Brecht's Verfremdungseffekt; Vogel credits Shklovsky.

choices: A timed exercise, often 48 hours, to write a play including assigned ingredients
A rehearsal technique for finding objectives
questions.explain: The constraints push writers past habit.

questions.q: A student finds her play only makes sense once you've seen the ending. Which Vogel phrase fits?
choices: Plot is the soul of tragedy
Time works backwards in the theatre
questions.explain: The ending rewrites what came before.

ideas: The Aristotelian arc is just one plot form among several: circular, backward and repetitive plays work differently.
Time works backwards in the theatre: the ending rewrites everything before it.
Give writers 48 hours and a list of odd ingredients, and they'll find structures they'd never plan.
